name: Ramakkalmedu
tagline: Wind‑swept ridge with windmills, wide Tamil Nadu panoramas and the Kuravan–Kurathi statue
summary: High‑range viewpoint in Idukki famous for persistent wind, windfarm silhouettes and wide clear‑air views — best in the dry season for sunrise and distant plains.
description: Ramakkalmedu is a high‑range viewpoint and small hill settlement in Idukki district. The ridge is famous for strong, steady winds, a line of wind turbines and wide panoramas that look east into the Cumbum/Theni plains of Tamil Nadu.

Visitors come for dramatic clear‑air views, wind‑sculpted grasslands, the twin Kuravan–Kurathi statue on the crest and short ridge walks. The windfarms and the turbines are part of the site’s character and photograph well against low winter sun.

Local tradition links the place to the Ramayana — the name Ramakkalmedu is told as ‘the hill where Rama set his foot’ — and the hill also hosts the large concrete Kuravan–Kurathi statue (sculpted by C.B. Jinan and erected in 2005).

Facilities are basic but official: a small DTPC tourism centre, parking and simple visitor amenities at the summit. Adventure visitors also use nearby Aamappara (tortoise rock) and off‑road jeep routes, though these have had regulatory changes since 2025 — confirm before you travel.
highlights: Wide eastward views over the Cumbum/Theni plains and distant Tamil Nadu towns
Persistent, photo‑worthy wind and visible wind‑farm turbines across the ridge
Kuravan–Kurathi twin statue (concrete monument on the summit)
Aamappara (tortoise rock) and short jeep/trek side‑trips — check operational status
Excellent sunrise and winter (dry season) clarity for landscape photography

sections.heading: Background
body: Ramakkalmedu stands on a western‑ghats ridge at roughly 9.79972°N, 77.23722°E and near 1,000 metres elevation. Strong winds have long defined the place; state wind surveys record a high annual mean and especially strong seasonal gusts.

The ridge includes private and state wind‑farm installations that supply local grids and visually mark the skyline. Tourism development is modest but growing: the DTPC maintains a small tourism centre and the area is on the district’s visitor circuit.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Walk the fenced viewpoints for wide eastward panoramas at sunrise or late afternoon; the wind and clear winter air give exceptional long‑distance visibility. The Kuravan–Kurathi statue crowns the ridge and makes a striking foreground for photos.

Explore nearby rock features such as Aamappara (the ‘tortoise rock’) and short ridge paths. Many visitors photograph the turbines, watch the wind sweep the grasslands, and combine Ramakkalmedu with nearby high‑range stops (Nedumkandam, Thookkupalam, Kattappana).

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: DTPC lists the Ramakkalmedu tourism centre open in daytime with a small entry fee; gates typically close by early evening, so plan arrivals well before sunset. The viewpoint is reached by surfaced hill road; short unsurfaced tracks lead to some rock features.

Off‑road jeep safaris up to Aamappara were affected by an Idukki district ban on unregulated off‑road jeeps in 2025 and services were restarted in phases with route approvals required. Before booking a jeep or planning an Aamappara visit, confirm current jeep operations with DTPC or the local counter.

latest.text: DTPC Idukki published an Expression of Interest inviting private partners to upgrade Ramakkalmedu tourism facilities (PPP proposal published 22 Sep 2025).

Idukki district ordered a ban on unregulated off‑road jeep safaris (impacting many Aamappara/Ramakkalmedu jeep runs); services restarted in phases under strict approvals but some routes remained closed — check current status before visiting.

visitorInfo.bestTime: December–March (dry season) for the clearest air, dramatic light and steadier viewing conditions.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Drive or take local buses toward Nedumkandam/Thookkupalam then follow the surfaced Thookkupalam–Ramakkalmedu road to the tourism centre; nearby towns: Thookkupalam (~8 km), Nedumkandam (~14 km), Kattappana (~23 km), Kumily (~48–50 km). Aamappara requires an approved jeep where that service is running—confirm with DTPC before you go.
etiquette: Wind is strong — wear a windproof layer and secure hats/gear; hold cameras and phones firmly.
Gate and tourism‑centre hours are daytime only; the hill road is unlit after dark — finish returns before sunset.
If you plan Aamappara or jeep trips, phone DTPC or the local counter to confirm approved jeep operations and safety rules.
Respect fenced viewpoints and stay well back from exposed escarpments; granite gets very slippery when wet.
